summary: RELOAD is a peer-to-peer signaling protocol that gives clients an abstract storage and messaging service across an overlay network of cooperating peers. It was designed to support peer-to-peer SIP (P2PSIP) but other applications can use it by defining new usages that specify what kinds of data to store.

plainLanguage.summary: RELOAD lets a group of computers route messages and store small records across a peer-to-peer network. Applications use the same base service and define their own data types and rules. Certificates and signatures identify who sent a message or wrote a record, while ICE helps nodes connect through NATs and firewalls.

questions: what is a node-id in reload
subtitle: A peer-to-peer overlay for routing messages and storing signed data without a central message router.

tldr.problem: Peer-to-peer applications need to find other nodes and store small records across a network whose members may not trust one another. Nodes also need a way to connect when they are behind network address translators or firewalls.
tldr.mechanism: RELOAD gives applications a common messaging and storage service over an overlay network. Nodes use identifiers and a topology plug-in to route requests, certificates and signatures to establish identity, and ICE to form connections through NATs.
tldr.outcome: Applications define usages that describe their data Kinds and access rules. RELOAD includes CHORD-RELOAD as a mandatory-to-implement topology; RFC 6940 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 6940 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the RELOAD base protocol; the SIP usage is described separately in a document referenced by the RFC.

sections.title: What RELOAD Provides
sections.content:
RFC 6940 defines REsource LOcation And Discovery (RELOAD), a peer-to-peer signaling protocol for the Internet. It provides messaging between nodes and a distributed service for storing and retrieving small, transient records. It was designed to support peer-to-peer Session Initiation Protocol (P2PSIP), but other applications can define usages for their own data.

An overlay instance is a partly connected network of nodes. Each node has a numeric Node-ID. Peers route messages and store data for other nodes; clients can use the overlay but do not route messages or store data on behalf of others. A Resource-ID names a place to store data, and the topology algorithm determines which peer is responsible for that place.
sections.plainLanguage: RELOAD is a common service that lets computers send messages and store small records across a network. Some nodes help route traffic and keep data for others; client nodes use the service without taking on those jobs.

sections.title: The Layers and Their Jobs
sections.content:
The Usage Layer defines application-specific data Kinds and how an application stores, secures, retrieves, and uses them. Message Transport manages end-to-end requests and responses, including retransmissions, while Storage handles Store and Fetch operations. These components expose a common messaging service to usages.

A Topology Plug-in implements the overlay algorithm, keeps its routing information, and chooses links. The Forwarding and Link Management Layer sends a message to its next peer and establishes connections, including through NATs using ICE. The Overlay Link Layer carries traffic directly between neighboring nodes; RFC 6940 specifies TLS and DTLS for this layer.

Reliability is split between layers. Message Transport retransmits requests end to end but does not provide congestion control. Forwarding and Link Management handles congestion control and reliability on each link.
sections.plainLanguage: RELOAD separates application data, message handling, routing, and direct connections into layers with different jobs. The routing plug-in chooses the next node, while the forwarding layer sends the message and manages each connection.

sections.title: Routing Requests and Returning Responses
sections.content:
A RELOAD message carries a Destination List that says where it should go. The list can name a node or, at its final position, a Resource-ID. Each forwarding peer adds the previous node to a Via List, so the destination can reverse that list and send its response back through the same peers. This required default is called symmetric recursive routing.

A peer may keep transaction state instead of carrying a full Via List, or replace list entries with an opaque identifier that only it can interpret. RELOAD also supports iterative routing: the sender asks a peer for the next hop with RouteQuery, then decides where to send the next request. A Resource-ID must be the only entry in a Destination List; the wildcard Node-ID is consumed by the receiving peer and is not forwarded.

The sender starts an end-to-end timer and may retransmit a request up to four times, for five transmissions in total, using the same transaction ID. A receiver must produce semantically equivalent responses to duplicate requests received within the maximum request lifetime, which defaults to 15 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each peer forwards a request toward a node or resource. The peers record enough route information for the response to travel back through them, or the sender can ask for each next hop itself.

If no response arrives, the sender can retry the request. A receiver must handle those retries as the same request while its request lifetime remains open.

sections.title: Message Parts and Signatures
sections.content:
Every RELOAD message has a Forwarding Header, Message Contents, and Security Block. The header contains information needed to route the message, including its overlay, protocol version, hop limit, transaction ID, Via List, and Destination List. The contents hold a request, response, or error. Integers are encoded in network byte order.

Request and response codes are paired: request codes are odd, and the matching response code is one greater. The error code is 0xFFFF. The Security Block carries certificates and a signature. Every message must be signed by its originator; intermediate peers do not verify the signature, but the destination verifies it after any fragments are reassembled. Implementations must support RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signatures with SHA-256.

The hop limit is reduced at each forwarding hop. Its initial value should be 100 and cannot exceed 100 unless the overlay configuration allows a different value. The transaction ID is a random 64-bit value used to match a response to its request and to reassemble fragments.
sections.plainLanguage:
A RELOAD message has routing information, the request or response, and a signature with the certificates needed to check it. The destination checks the signature after it has received all parts of the message.

The hop limit prevents a message from traveling forever. A shared transaction number lets the sender match the reply to the request.

sections.title: Forming Connections Between Nodes
sections.content:
Attach establishes a direct RELOAD link between two nodes. The initiating node sends ICE connection candidates through the overlay; the other node returns its candidates, and both nodes run ICE connectivity checks. RELOAD implementations must support full ICE. No-ICE link protocols are also defined for configured overlays where ICE is not used.

Attaching alone does not make a connection available for routing messages through one node to other peers. An Update changes routing information, and a peer must not forward through a new connection until it has the required routing state. This separation lets a client attach without joining the overlay as a peer. AppAttach uses a separate connection for an application protocol, and Ping tests connectivity.

RELOAD specifies DTLS over UDP with Simple Reliability, TLS over TCP with a framing header and no ICE, and DTLS over UDP with Simple Reliability and no ICE. On unreliable links, Simple Reliability acknowledges each message and retransmits it hop by hop. Large messages can be split into fragments along the route, but only the final destination reassembles them.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two nodes exchange connection details through RELOAD, then use ICE to check whether they can communicate directly. A direct connection becomes a route for other traffic only after the overlay's Update process supplies the needed routing information.

RELOAD can acknowledge and resend messages on each link. If a message is too large for a link, nodes can split it, and the destination puts the pieces back together.

sections.title: Storing and Retrieving Data
sections.content:
A Resource-ID can hold data of several Kinds. Each Kind has a 32-bit Kind-ID, a data model, and an access-control policy. RELOAD defines three data models: a single value that a new value replaces, an array addressed by a zero-based index, and a dictionary addressed by a key.

Each StoredData value includes its storage time, lifetime, contents, and writer's signature. A peer rejects a value with an older storage time than the one it would replace, which helps prevent rollback. Store requests covering multiple Kinds are atomic: if one part fails, the peer restores the previous state. A generation counter lets a writer check the current state before updating it.

Store writes values, Fetch retrieves them, Stat returns metadata, and Find reports the closest known Resource-ID for a Kind. RELOAD has no separate Remove operation; a writer stores a signed value marked as nonexistent instead. The base protocol also defines a Certificate Store Usage and a TURN Server Usage.
sections.plainLanguage:
Applications choose a Kind for each type of record and use one of RELOAD's storage models. A signed record includes a time and a lifetime, so peers can reject older replacements and stop treating expired data as valid.

Applications can write, retrieve, inspect, or locate records. To remove a value, its owner stores a signed entry that says the value no longer exists.

sections.title: The CHORD-RELOAD Topology
sections.content:
RELOAD permits different topology plug-ins, but every implementation must support CHORD-RELOAD, its adaptation of the Chord distributed hash table. Peers are arranged in a ring. Each peer keeps a Neighbor Table of nearby peers and a Finger Table of peers at increasingly distant positions around the ring. The neighbor links maintain the ring; finger links help locate a destination in logarithmic time.

In CHORD-RELOAD, a peer is responsible for Resource-IDs between its previous peer's Node-ID and its own Node-ID, including its own identifier. A Resource-ID is formed with SHA-1 truncated to its most significant 128 bits. To forward a request, a peer chooses a routing-table entry that advances toward the destination.

The responsible peer stores data locally and sends replicas to its successor and that peer's successor. These replicas help if a peer fails, but the RFC says this sequential replication does not protect against malicious peers. Joining involves connecting to an admitting peer, receiving the data for the new range, and exchanging updates; the joining peer must connect to its required neighbors before announcing itself in the ring.
sections.plainLanguage:
CHORD-RELOAD arranges peers in a ring and gives each peer nearby contacts plus links farther around the ring. These links let a peer move a request toward the peer responsible for a resource.

The responsible peer stores the data and sends copies to two successors. Those copies help with peer failures, but do not stop a malicious peer from withholding data.

sections.title: Configuration, Enrollment, and Joining
sections.content:
A node starts with an overlay name and retrieves a Configuration Document, usually by looking up a configuration server with DNS and fetching the document over HTTPS. The document gives overlay parameters such as trust anchors, enrollment servers, bootstrap nodes, and the topology plug-in. It contains security-critical information and must be obtained securely.

If the overlay uses centralized enrollment, the node sends a certificate request to the enrollment server over HTTPS. The returned certificate identifies the permitted Node-ID or IDs and the user's name. The enrollment server should return the same Node-IDs when the same user renews a certificate. In an overlay that permits self-signed certificates, a node can generate its own identity; the RFC limits this approach to less-trusting security settings.

To join, the node first connects to a bootstrap node and sends an Attach request directed to the resource just after its Node-ID. The overlay algorithm then connects it to peers, transfers the data it will become responsible for, and updates routing information. A client does not perform the peer-joining steps.
sections.plainLanguage:
A new node gets the overlay's settings before it connects. If the overlay requires enrollment, a server issues a certificate that identifies the node and the user.

The node contacts a bootstrap peer, then follows the topology's process to connect, receive its share of stored data, and join routing. A client can use the overlay without joining as a peer.

sections.title: Security Protections and Their Limits
sections.content:
RELOAD protects communication at the link, message, and stored-object levels. TLS or DTLS secures connections between peers; the originator signs each message; and the writer signs each stored value. Certificate-based security is required. A responsible peer checks whether the writer's certificate permits the requested operation for that Kind and Resource-ID.

Central enrollment assigns random Node-IDs and limits who can join, which makes Sybil attacks harder and deters some Eclipse attacks. Self-signed certificates weaken these protections and are suitable only for closed groups of mutually trusting users. An optional shared-secret mode controls who can form connections, but password-derived keys with TLS-PSK can be vulnerable to dictionary attacks; the RFC recommends TLS-SRP when passwords are used.

Signatures can reveal tampering, but they cannot force a peer to store or return data. A peer can also return only some values in a multi-valued record. Replicated records and parallel searches can reduce the effect of withholding, while routing attacks can still disrupt service. The RFC recommends limiting the initial hop count and discarding destination lists with duplicate entries to reduce routing-loop abuse.
sections.plainLanguage:
Certificates establish which nodes may participate, and signatures let a receiver check who sent a message or wrote a value. These checks can expose changes, but cannot make a peer keep or return data.

Replication and parallel searches can reduce the effect of a peer that withholds data. RELOAD's protections limit some attacks, but do not eliminate routing disruption or attacks by compromised members.
